data.title: DSC Partners with JAPANCARS to Channel China’s Used Cars to Global Dealers
data.description:
SINGAPORE, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- DSC Holdings Ltd. (“DSC” or the “Company”) , the AI application infrastructure for China’s used car industry, today announced a vehicle-sourcing partnership with Japanese automotive trading company JAPANCARS CO., LTD. (“JAPANCARS”). The partnership went live on November 18, 2026, and is conducted through DASOUCHE PTE. LTD., the Company’s Singapore-based overseas headquarters. JAPANCARS operates JAPANCARS Exporter Platform, a vehicle export marketplace serving dealers worldwide. Through the partnership, JAPANCARS and its dealer clients can tap directly into the vast inventory offered by Chinese used car dealers, marking a significant step in DSC’s effort to connect China’s used car supply with global distribution networks.

For China’s used car industry, this partnership builds a direct and efficient route to overseas markets. China’s massive used car supply is spread across several hundred thousand dealers, nearly all of which are small and mid-sized independent businesses, which makes cross-border used car trades difficult and inefficient. Few dealers have reliable relationships with overseas buyers, and most lack the standardized vehicle data, language capabilities and fulfillment capacity that cross-border trade demands. As a long-time partner to China’s used car dealers, DSC aims to remove those barriers. Its platform gives dealers a consolidated point of entry to overseas marketplaces, allowing them to reach buyers worldwide without painstakingly building export channels of their own. The result is a shift from piecemeal, one-to-one transactions to a scaled channel connecting hundreds of thousands of Chinese dealers with buyers around the world. This partnership with JAPANCARS is expected to contribute to DSC’s digitalization solutions revenue and drive demand for related transaction services.

JAPANCARS has built a well-established automotive trading business spanning Japan, Southeast Asia and North America, serving more than 2,500 dealers in 46 countries to date. International dealers seeking to purchase inventory across multiple Chinese sellers have typically needed to reach out to each of the sellers separately. This partnership with DSC gives JAPANCARS’ worldwide clients one place to browse China’s deep pool of vehicle inventory and source the models that suit their local demand.

“International expansion is a clear, long-term strategy for DSC,” said Liyu Zhang, Senior Vice President of DSC. “Teaming up with JAPANCARS to bring high-quality Chinese used cars to overseas buyers is an encouraging start. We will keep equipping our dealers to sell abroad, smoothing their path into international markets, and helping China’s used cars build a strong presence worldwide.”

“Used car exports hinge on understanding overseas demand and local pricing,” said Terry On, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of JAPANCARS. “Through our partnership with DSC, we act as a conduit, helping overseas buyers find the right Chinese used cars for their markets while showing Chinese dealers which models can sell abroad.”

About DSC

DSC is the AI application infrastructure for China’s used car industry. Since 2021, DSC has consistently held more than 90% market share in operating systems for China’s used car dealers, according to CIC, giving it deep connections with dealers nationwide and exclusive access to massive, granular, real-time industry data. Building on this digital infrastructure, DSC provides used car dealers with essential transaction services across their workflows. DSC’s platform also engages and benefits thousands of dealer collaborators, including used car inspectors, transporters and other internet platform service providers, forming an ecosystem with used car dealers at its center.

About JAPANCARS

Founded in 2010 and headquartered in Kanagawa Prefecture, JAPANCARS is a B2B exporter and trader of new and used vehicles, serving customers worldwide from its base in Japan. Its JAPANCARS Exporter Platform gives clients direct access to used car auctions, where they can choose from tens of thousands of vehicles on offer each day, with JAPANCARS supporting them through bidding, condition inspection and shipping.

Forward-Looking Statements

This press release contains forward-looking statements concerning the future direction of the parties’ cooperation and plans to launch related services. These statements are based on current expectations and are subject to a number of factors, including market conditions, regulatory requirements and the progress of execution. Actual results may differ from those expressed or implied in these statements. Except as required by law, DSC undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements.

data.title: Australia, NZ dollars find support as yield gap remains a drag
data.description:
By Wayne Cole

The Australian and New Zealand dollars found a sliver of support on Friday after a bruising month in which a global technology-led selloff soured risk sentiment and eroded the currencies' yield advantage over the greenback.

The Aussie was a shade firmer at $0.6643 , having inched up 0.1% overnight. It remains down 5.5% this month and, if losses hold, is headed for its worst monthly performance since late 2022. Chart support lies around $0.6560 and $0.6422, with resistance at $0.6665 and $0.6855.

The currency has been undermined by a sharp shift in rate expectations after a surprisingly weak jobs report led markets to price in cuts for 2027, reversing part of this year's 125-basis-point tightening in market pricing.

Futures imply around a 50% chance of a quarter-point easing in the 4.85% cash rate by May, and a move to 4.60% is fully priced by August. (0#AUDIRPR)

At the same time, strong US data has led investors to price at least two more hikes from the Federal Reserve, while Australian bond yields have fallen below those on Treasuries.

"If Australian bond yields are unable to re-establish a positive differential over US equivalents, AUD/USD should struggle to sustain gains much above $0.65 on a sustainable basis," said Ray Attrill, head of FX strategy at NAB.

"This is reflected in our forecast track, which has a low point of $0.64 in Q3 2027, but allows for a $0.62-$0.69 range, while under a severe risk-off scenario, we shouldn't discount the risk of a revisit to, or below, $0.60."

Attrill sees the kiwi dollar ending the year around $0.5500, where it is now, before rising slowly over 2027 to $0.5900 as the Reserve Bank of New Zealand lifts rates.

Markets imply an 83% chance the RBNZ will hike by a quarter point to 3.0% in December, and reach 3.5% in the second half of next year. <0$NZDIRPR>

The kiwi was up 0.2% at $0.5469 on Friday, partly on relief a lengthy vote count had left the coalition government in pole position to remain in power, albeit with the support of a minor centrist party.

The currency is still down 2.6% for the month so far and is set for a third consecutive monthly decline. Support lies at the recent trough of $0.5434, a low not seen since early 2009, with resistance around $0.5495.

data.title: Shares find footing after bruising month, dollar set for third monthly gain
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nikkei up 0.7%, Nasdaq futures climb 1%
  • Dollar up 1.8% this month against its major peers
  • Kiwi edges higher after election results suggest status quo

By Stella Qiu

Asian shares were set to end a bruising month on a steadier note as a holiday lull offered some respite from AI jitters, while the dollar reigned supreme, riding a wave of safe-haven demand and rate hike bets towards a third month of gains.

Oil prices were headed for the first weekly rise in four on renewed concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures slipped 0.4% on Friday to $96.14 a barrel, but were still up 3.9% for the week. For the month, they were down 18%.

Wall Street was closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, but in Asia, S&P 500 futures were up 0.8% and Nasdaq futures were 1% higher.

Japan's Nikkei rose 0.7% to bring its gains for the week to 2.7%, clawing back only a fraction of its 8.4% loss for the month. Data showed on Friday that core inflation in Tokyo hit a 16-month high in November, bolstering the case for an interest rate hike from the Bank of Japan as soon as next month.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MIAPJ0000PUS) edged up 0.5% to end the week 1.9% higher. It was still down 8.2% for the month.

Shares in South Korea rallied 2% and China's blue chips slipped 0.2%, after hitting the lowest level since June 2025 a day earlier.

"Barring a big shock that severely rattles a thin market, November is practically in the books and the markets limp into December where a seasonal 'Santa Rally' currently appears elusive," said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com.

"For as long as the markets remain unsure about the growth trajectory for AI and lack clarity about where US rates may peak, uncertainty and therefore volatility is liable to remain elevated."

Tech giant Nvidia remained a source of unease after S&P put its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade. The chipmaker told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported.

Elsewhere in tech, Elon Musk said that every child in the US would receive two shares in his space and AI company SpaceX , pledging a gift worth some $18 billion.

DOLLAR REIGNS

The US dollar was headed to its third monthly gain on Friday, up 1.8% against its major peers at 103.8. It has been supported by expectations that the Federal Reserve is almost certain to lift interest rates in December, as well as safe-haven flows from the selloff in equities.

Futures imply a 99% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, but speculation of a half-point increase has faded. (0#USDIRPR)

The euro was last flat at $1.0964 , after news that Spanish central banking veteran Pablo Hernández de Cos would become the next European Central Bank president, a move that was well telegraphed and suggested policy continuity.

The kiwi edged up 0.2% to $0.5482 after New Zealand's ruling centre-right coalition fell short of a parliamentary majority, leaving it reliant on negotiations with the centrist Opportunity Party to stay in power.

Bond investors are wondering if the broad losses in global stocks this month coupled with doubts about the durability of AI-driven business investment might temper the hawkishness of central banks.

"The Fed could, of course, still blink," said David Rees, chief economist at Schroders. "But a Fed put would not necessarily be unambiguously positive for markets."

"If growth and inflation data remain firm, in a game of cat and mouse markets could soon begin pricing a more hawkish Fed back in, potentially setting off the same chain of events all over again."

Two-year Treasury yields (US2YT=RR) rose 3 basis points to 4.6705% as the cash market reopened after the US holiday. They were up 6 bps this week.

Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields rose 4 bps to 4.8918%, but were down 2 bps for the week.

data.title: Japanese Market Notably Higher
data.description:
TOKYO (dpa-AFX) - The Japanese market is notably higher on Friday, extending the gains in the previous session, following the positive cues from European markets and lack of cues from Wall Street overnight. The Nikkei 225 is moving up to near the 57,750 level, with gains in exporters, automakers and technology stocks partially offset by weakness in index heavyweights.

The benchmark Nikkei 225 Index is up 248.36 points or 0.43 percent to 57,747.52, after touching a high of 57,994.39 earlier. Japanese shares ended significantly higher on Thursday.

Market heavyweight SoftBank Group is losing almost 3 percent and Uniqlo operator Fast Retailing is edging down 0.3 percent. Among automakers, Toyota is gaining almost 1 percent and Honda is adding more than 1 percent.

In the tech space, Advantest is losing almost 1 percent and Tokyo Electron is declining almost 3 percent, while Screen Holdings is gaining more than 1 percent.

In the banking sector, Mizuho Financial is advancing almost 3 percent, while Mitsubishi UFJ Financial and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial are gaining almost 2 percent each.

Among the major exporters, Sony is losing almost 2 percent, while Mitsubishi Electric is advancing almost 3 percent, Canon is edging up 0.3 percent and Panasonic is gaining almost 2 percent.

Among other major gainers, Socionext is jumping more than 6 percent, while IHI, Furukawa Electric and Resonac Holdings are surging almost 6 percent each. Kioxia Holdings is gaining more than 5 percent, while Japan Steel Works, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Sumitomo Heavy Industries and Chubu Electric Power are advancing more than 4 percent each. Tokyo Electric, Mitsui Kinzoku and Idemitsu Kosan are adding almost 4 percent each, while Dowa Holdings and ENEOS Holdings are up more than 3 percent each.

Conversely, Recruit Holdings is losing more than 3 percent.

In economic news, core consumer prices in Tokyo's central wards increased 2.9 percent on year in November 2026, accelerating from a 2.6 percent rise in October but falling short of expectations of 3.0 percent. It was the fastest increase since July 2025 and remained above the Bank of Japan's 2 percent target for the third consecutive month

Meanwhile, the CPI, which excludes volatile fresh food and energy prices, rose 2.5 percent on year, down from 2.6 percent in October and below forecasts of 3.0 percent, marking the slowest pace in three months.

In the currency market, the U.S. dollar is trading in the lower 159 yen-range on Friday.

On Wall Street, the markets were closed for Thanksgiving Day on Thursday after closing mixed on Wednesday.

The major European markets moved to the upside on the day. The German DAX rallied 2 percent, France's CAC 40 surged 1.7 percent and the U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 1.5 percent.

Crude oil prices rose on Thursday to extend the gains in the previous session amid supply concerns after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and two ships hit mines laid by the Iranian's in the Strait of Hormuz. The US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained $0.35 or 0.4 percent to $84.03 a barrel.

data.title: Asian Markets Mostly Higher as Sentiment Stabilizes
data.description:
By Sherry Qin

Asian markets were mostly higher Friday, tracking gains in U.S. stock futures as sentiment around artificial intelligence stabilized.

"U.S. markets were closed for Thanksgiving, leaving global markets to trade largely off the late recovery on Wall Street in Wednesday's session," said Westpac's Neha Sharma in an email.

Asian markets have also taken cues from stronger U.S. stock futures. E-mini Nasdaq futures were up 1.3%, while contracts tied to the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.0% and 0.7%, respectively.

South Korea's Kospi rose 1.65% and Japan's Nikkei Stock Average rose 0.7%. China's Shanghai Composite Index added 0.2% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 0.2% higher. However, Taiwan's Taiex bucked the trend to drop 0.3%.

The gains came even as Nvidia ordered its manufacturing partners to pause shipments to four Southeast Asian countries, after the U.S. escalated its push to keep the company's AI chips out of China's hands, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Oil prices were mixed after rallying overnight. Iran has stepped up its strikes targeting some of its Gulf neighbors and ships trying to get oil and natural gas out through the Strait of Hormuz. Most recently, an Iranian drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italians performing maintenance on antidrone equipment, authorities said.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthi militant group attacked Saudi Arabia's Jazan oil refinery on Thursday and killed one worker, the kingdom's Ministry of Energy said in a statement.

The attacks offset hopes of a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, ANZ Research analysts said in a note.

However, U.S. commercial crude oil inventories rose for a third consecutive week in the seven days through Nov. 20, while gasoline and distillate stockpiles also increased, according to the latest data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude-oil futures rose 2.1% to $85.41 a barrel, while front-month Brent was down 0.4% at $96.20 a barrel, according to ICE data.

Write to Sherry Qin at sherry.qin@wsj.com

data.title: They Pledged to Give Away 10% of Their Income. Now They're AI Billionaires. — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Cohen and Berber Jin | Graphics by Jason French

The movement that helped shape the hottest AI company in the world began with 23 people.

On a Saturday in November 2009, a small group of friends met in a cramped room at the University of Oxford. They were moral philosophers, development economists, bioethicists, doctors, lawyers and students — and they were about to do something that sounded a little nuts.

That day, they made a pledge to give away 10% of their income for the rest of their working lives. They would direct it to charities that could most effectively fight poverty in the developing world.

Since then, the 10% Pledge has become more influential than anyone at the first meeting could have possibly imagined. It has expanded to a wider range of causes and spread far beyond Oxford, growing from a society called Giving What We Can that could fit in a classroom to a global network of nearly 11,500 people.

Some of them can now give millions of dollars — even billions.

Dario Amodei, for one, took the pledge back when he was a student in 2010. These days, Member No. 43 is better known by another designation: CEO of Anthropic.

Nobody at the company was earlier to the 10% Pledge than Amodei himself, but at least 50 current and former Anthropic employees are on the list of pledgers, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis.

They include co-founders Tom Brown (No. 1,214) and Jack Clark (No. 4,002), plus Amanda Askell (No. 67), who wrote Claude's constitution and teaches morals to AI models, and Evan Hubinger (No. 2,591), who recently warned those models might kill us all. Also on the list is Jacob Coxon (No. 3,970), who quit the company to raise alarms about superintelligence racing beyond human control.

As one of the world's richest people, Amodei is no longer satisfied with giving away 10% of his income. Before the AI lab went public, Anthropic's seven founders made a pledge of their own: to donate 80% of their equity to charity. That stock is collectively worth more than $100 billion.

The company also runs a generous matching program for employees who donate their shares. Before the largest IPO in history, Anthropic called it a "reflection of the values that define our culture."

The company's earliest employees believed that artificial intelligence could one day grow powerful enough to be dangerous, and that trying to build it safely would be the most important thing they could do in their lifetimes. Many of them also believed in effective altruism, the movement the 10% Pledge helped launch. They wanted to use evidence and reason to do the most good.

Compared with their peers in Silicon Valley, they didn't care nearly as much about making money for themselves. Now they have lots of it — and they're deciding how to give it away.

In recent months, employees have been inviting charitable groups to Anthropic's unmarked offices in downtown San Francisco to discuss philanthropic strategies. Some are planning to funnel the money they have made from AI to reduce catastrophic and existential risks caused by AI, all while they keep racing to build AI.

"These people are developing a product with enormous potential to do good and enormous potential to do bad," said philosopher Peter Singer (No. 16). "Presumably, they are trying to tilt the odds as much as they can so that it does more good."

Long before he took the pledge, Singer helped inspire perhaps the most famous philosophy to emerge from Oxford since the days of John Locke.

In the 1970s, he published an essay called "Famine, Affluence and Morality" that argued people in rich countries have a moral obligation to give far more to help the poor. Decades later, he received an unusual email in 2007 from a graduate student named Toby Ord.

"He wasn't disputing the argument or saying it was too demanding," Singer said. "He wanted to start a movement to make more people aware of the argument and live in accordance with that argument."

Ord had a grand vision for a community of people who wanted to give more — and give more effectively.

Effective giving was built on a few simple concepts: giving a lot is easier than you think, giving to high-impact charities makes those donations more powerful, and most people dramatically underestimate the difference that a single person can make. If you donated $15, for example, you could buy a toy for one child. But with that same $15, you could buy a year's worth of clean water for 10 children.

Ord's plans were much bigger than $15. He promised to give away every penny he earned above GBP20,000 a year, which would work out to GBP1 million over his career. Back in 2009, he said there was only one indulgence he found tempting: the iPhone.

That year, Ord met a graduate student named Will MacAskill. Their first conversation at Oxford took place in a garden that doubles as a graveyard. And as they discussed Ord's vow, MacAskill came alive.

Within months, they launched the Giving What We Can pledge.

The pledge is not a binding contract but an oath — "a public declaration of lasting commitment," as the organization puts it — and many pledgers signal their commitment through an orange diamond emoji on their social-media profiles. At first, every sign-up felt momentous, and the British press was skeptical there would be many.

"They were excited to talk to me," Ord said later. "But they kept saying: 'No one's really going to do this, are they?'"

As it turned out, one of the first to do it was the future CEO of a trillion-dollar company.

Dario Amodei felt that giving away a big chunk of his income was an important part of his personal mission to "make the world a better place," he wrote in 2010, when he added his name to the pledge. At that time, almost nobody in America had even heard of it. He is still listed between a Canadian therapist (No. 42) and a British radiotherapy physicist (No. 44).

As the pledge's birthplace, Oxford blossomed into the spiritual home of effective altruism, pulling in true believers and earnest young people with huge ambitions. Among them were Leopold Aschenbrenner, the Anthropic investor whose hedge fund recently had a blowup, and Avital Balwit (No. 4,708), his wife and Amodei's chief of staff.

Anthropic's CEO made his fortune long after taking the pledge. Others were inspired by the pledge to make a fortune.

They embraced a practice called "earn to give," taking lucrative jobs in tech and finance so they could donate more. The strategy was evangelized by MacAskill, who once refused to get a haircut because it struck him as an unnecessary expense. His most notable acolyte was a crypto tycoon also allergic to haircuts: Sam Bankman-Fried (No. 1,888). MacAskill later advised Bankman-Fried's foundation, which hoped to distribute up to $1 billion in 2022 and do "as much good as we can for the future of the world."

Their future didn't go as planned. When FTX collapsed into bankruptcy and Bankman-Fried went to prison, the fallout turned effective altruism radioactive. After its own judicial process, Giving What We Can ruled that Bankman-Fried violated the community's norms and his name was removed from the pledge's membership list, which now skips from 1,887 to 1,889.

Since then, effective altruism has roared back, 10% Pledge sign-ups have picked up and the Giving What We Can community has now given away a total of more than $500 million.

Anthropic's employees may be among the wealthiest people who have taken the pledge, but they represent a small minority of a coalition across 120 countries that includes U.S. military veterans, Australian phys-ed teachers, Norwegian entrepreneurs, a tennis player who won an Olympic medal and an economist who won the Nobel Prize.

"There are people earning a lot of money," said Sjir Hoeijmakers (No. 4,736), the CEO of Giving What We Can, which runs the pledge, "but also people earning very little money."

Since that first meeting in Oxford, the pledge has changed in several ways. The most consequential one can be found in the language of the pledge itself.

In 2014, "fight poverty in developing countries" became "improve the lives of others." Now members are free to give their money wherever they believe it will have the maximum impact.

Global health remains the most popular cause, with almost half of their donations last year going to efforts like fighting malaria. In the age of AI, some have turned their attention to reducing catastrophic risks. They also give to animal welfare, which has a devoted following inside Anthropic.

Many early employees are vegetarians, including Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela, Anthropic's co-founder and president. Others fondly remember an AI model released more than two years ago that displayed an unusually high level of concern for animals. One research recruiter at the company wrote in her bio at a recent effective-altruism conference that she planned to donate 25% of her equity to improving the lives of farm animals.

Last year, the Giving What We Can organization set a target of one million pledgers, which it called a "big, hairy, audacious goal." Singer calls it not nearly audacious enough.

"There must be a billion people," he said, "who could quite comfortably do that without any real sacrifice."

As it happens, he's visiting San Francisco next month and planning to meet with the 10% Pledgers who can now give more than almost everyone: Anthropic employees.

data.title: The Savvy Showmanship That Helps Jensen Huang Always Come Out on Top — WSJ
data.description:
By Erich Schwartzel

The table tennis community of Portland, Ore., had never seen anything like him.

Standing 5'3" and weighing 105 pounds, 14-year-old Jen-Hsun Huang was a ping pong phenom. After he showed up at the city's Paddle Palace, its owner, Lou Bochenski, was telling Sports Illustrated that he was the most promising junior player to ever compete in the Northwest.

"I suggest you watch out for him," Bochenski wrote in a letter to the editor.

Huang had only started playing the sport three months earlier — and the star student told reporters that he hoped to grow up to become a nuclear engineer.

Huang was a quick study — with a fueling ambition for the next bigger stage, no matter what stage he had already ascended. During the early days of Nvidia, he announced every deal with fanfare to raise the upstart company's profile as fast as possible. By his 30s, he was stopped for autographs by videogame enthusiasts.

And when Nvidia took Huang to the highest echelons of corporate influence and geopolitical sway, the CEO used a nerdy job to cast himself as an industry celebrity, business titan and Washington power player. Through doggedness and showmanship, Jen-Hsun became Jensen — famous enough in some circles to be known by one name.

Then last month, it appeared to all come crashing down. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman that U.S. government officials believed was working with China's premier spy agency. The affair, along with a second relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, would cost Huang his job, send the stock tumbling and realign interests in D.C. over the China-U. S. competition shaping the 21st century.

When it looked like Huang's career at Nvidia was finished, Jon Peddie, a longtime friend of Huang's, observed: "Maybe Jensen is Icarus, and the wax is melting."

It wasn't. On Monday, Nvidia's board hired Huang back as CEO, following an intervention by President Trump. The stock surged. Hundreds of employees greeted their former boss with cheers and chants of his name. One woman hugged him, wiping away tears.

Huang apologized to employees. "I made some terrible mistakes," he said, adding that he is attending daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

Nvidia's board said it was confident that having Huang as CEO "poses no national security risk," but to some lawmakers, his reinstatement has become a glaring example of corruption in the Trump era — one they still plan to investigate.

Huang's story has been an American one: the son of immigrants, sent to the U.S. with only an older brother and poor English, who goes on to co-found what was for a time the most valuable company on Earth.

Interviews with friends and associates who have known him since his pre-Nvidia days describe an executive of singular intensity and savvy — with an unrelenting ability to make the most of any situation. Employees in recent interviews — and in some lawsuits — have also described a shadow side to Huang's ambition, describing a workplace where he excoriated subordinates and ruled with a fearsome temper. His centrality to Nvidia — from its operations to its public image — is extreme even by the standards of an industry accustomed to the likes of Elon Musk or Steve Jobs defining their own enterprises.

The seeds of his success at Nvidia can be found in unlikely places — a Denny's in Oregon where he bused tables in high school, a videogame convention where he was treated like a god. But so can the signs of a potential downfall, most notably in an embrace of showmanship and a tendency to stretch the boundaries of the power he wields.

Peddie, an expert in computer graphics, first met Huang when Huang called him in the early 1990s for advice about a company he was thinking of starting — the company that would become Nvidia.

There were times, Peddie said, when he listened to Huang's ambition and thought to himself: "He's toast, this isn't going to work."

But Wednesday, with his friend reinstated as CEO, Peddie remembered the slogan he had long ago ascribed to Huang:

"Jensen will always pull a rabbit out of a hat."

Huang was only 10 years old when he first found himself in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Born in Taiwan, he had been living in Thailand when his parents sent him and his older brother to live with relatives in the U.S. Those relatives, believing they were enrolling the siblings in a prestigious boarding school, sent them to the Oneida Baptist Institute in rural Kentucky.

It was not a prestigious boarding school. It was a school for juvenile delinquents, where classmates carried knives to class.

Huang eventually reunited with his parents and settled in the Portland area, where, in addition to table tennis, he gorged on American culture: "The Partridge Family," Snickers bars, "Speed Racer." Before coming to the U.S., he had never walked into a house with carpet.

A straight-A student, he enrolled at Oregon State University because a friend from high school was going there, he told Condoleezza Rice in a conversation the two recorded earlier this year.

In a yearbook photo, he posed with the other members of Eta Kappa Nu, the honorary fraternity for electrical engineering students. His outfit — an argyle sweater, worn over a shirt and tie — is a far cry from the Tom Ford leather jackets that would become his signature look.

At Oregon State, he would meet his future wife, Lori Huang, one of three women in the school's engineering class of 250. In interviews, Huang would note that Lori never complained about the long hours that building Nvidia kept him from home.

By choosing a career in chips, Huang was pursuing what at one time was considered the geekiest of engineering fields. But when he and two co-founders started Nvidia in 1993, they quickly established a name for themselves with a product that compressed power and allowed even established players to elevate their software offerings.

Brad Silverberg was working at one of those established players — Microsoft, where he was a senior vice president overseeing several signature products, including Windows 95.

When he met Huang, Microsoft's gaming division was lagging behind its competitors. Huang's pitch: Our chips can help you catch up.

"His enthusiasm was always so infectious," said Silverberg in an interview. "It just made us want to work 28 hours a day."

Inking agreements with Microsoft, Sega and other notable partners put Nvidia on the map — something Huang was eager to do, usually through an ongoing stream of press releases trumpeting each deal.

Sega tapped Nvidia to build what it hoped would be a hit product to rival PlayStation, after executive Shoichiro Irimajiri met with Huang and was impressed by his passion and vision. That work with Sega gave a critical boost to Nvidia, before a flawed strategy for rendering images nearly sank the company. Sega ultimately offered a $5 million lifeline, taking a stake in the company. Huang traveled to Japan to meet with senior Sega leaders and keep the partnership alive.

With that cash infusion, Nvidia scrambled to create the breakthrough chip released in 1997.

That new Nvidia chip allowed videogames to graduate from pixelated graphics to photo-realistic displays. Characters on screen looked more humanlike than ever — in the 1998 hit "Half-Life," players aimed their rifles at characters whose eyes followed the shooter as he moved through the room. Nvidia went public the next year.

The gaming world wasn't as buttoned-up as other parts of Silicon Valley; the crew leading Microsoft's games effort was known as "the Beastie Boys." Huang embraced that side of the work too, showing up to conventions in some cases dressed in his products, like when he arrived at the 2009 Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas wearing 3-D glasses and bearing a Rockband guitar, which he held over his head and pretended to shred.

"He was a rock star in that world," Silverberg said.

Speaking with Charlie Rose in 2009, Huang described his work in simple but poetic terms: "We take a bunch of numbers and a ton of data...and we make you imagine you're seeing the world."

Then came what Huang would describe as the "big bang."

Research into neural networks and artificial intelligence revealed another use for Nvidia chips — the ability to scale the computing power needed to build and train large language models. Huang wasn't just selling pickaxes during the gold rush, but providing buyers with a path toward the realization of the chips' power.

As Nvidia's reach and valuation grew, first to $1 trillion and eventually north of $5 trillion, Huang's reputation as a micromanaging obsessive boss did too. He managed 60 direct reports, a structure that made it nearly impossible to replace him, and said as recently as this past week that he doesn't think succession planning makes sense for Nvidia.

He was known to dress down subordinates in meetings and berate staff for ideas he saw as lacking. In group meetings, they said he sometimes used the term "dead-face" to describe staffers' blank expressions after he scolded them, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Nvidia also became something of a family company, with Huang's son, daughter and son-in-law all working there — his daughter served as his chief of staff. Since news of her father's affairs have roiled the company, colleagues have accused her of inheriting her father's management style, berating employees and wielding power through intimidation.

Huang's singular drive also earned him the loyalty of staff eager to do cutting-edge work and global leaders taken by his smarts and influence. He won the affection of President Trump, who didn't know Huang's name at the start of his second term, but would eventually turn to him for advice — and allow the exports he sought of powerful chips to China.

data.title: Encore Season: Agoda Sees Searches for Jakarta Stays More Than Triple as the BTS World Tour 'Arirang' Heads to Southeast Asia
data.description:
SINGAPORE, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Searches on digital travel platform Agoda for Jakarta stays on the nights K-pop group BTS plays Gelora Bung Karno Main Stadium are up 205% year on year. Fans heading to Singapore's four shows are searching 63% more than last year for those dates, Bangkok's three show nights are up 50%, and Kuala Lumpur's 12 and 13 December show weekend is up 26%.

BTS brings its 'Arirang' world tour to Southeast Asia this December, performing at Rajamangala National Stadium in Bangkok on 3, 5 and 6 December, TM Stadium Nasional in Kuala Lumpur on 12 and 13 December, Singapore's National Stadium on 17, 19, 20 and 22 December, and Jakarta on 26, 27 and 29 December. For many fans, a ticket is only half of the plan. The other half is a bed close enough to make the walk home after the encore an easy one, and Agoda's search data shows that fans are already getting excited about their stays.

Interest Builds in Concert Host Cities

Agoda looked at searches made between 90 and 30 days before each city's first show, for stays on the concert dates, and compared them with searches made over the same dates a year earlier. In that window, Jakarta searches more than tripled, up 205%, Singapore rose 63%, Bangkok 50% and Kuala Lumpur 26%. In Jakarta, the shows coincide with the year-end holidays.

Where the Fans Are Coming From

  • Bangkok: local fans lead, followed by travellers from Vietnam, Singapore, Japan and Malaysia.
  • Kuala Lumpur: local fans lead, followed by travelers from Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines.
  • Singapore: travelers from the Philippines lead, followed by Indonesia, local fans, Malaysia and Thailand.
  • Jakarta: local fans lead, followed by travelers from Malaysia, Singapore, Japan and the Philippines.

Andrew Smith, Senior Vice President, Supply at Agoda, shared, "Fans don't just buy a ticket. They plan a trip around it, and our search data shows that fans are seeking the perfect stay to make the most of the BTS World Tour's arrival in Southeast Asia. In every host city, local fans are searching alongside travelers from across the region. Whether fans are traveling across borders, coming from a different city, or simply looking for accommodation closer to the venue, Agoda lets them compare stays based on their preferences and add flights to the same booking, all in one place."

Where to Stay: A Show Night Neighborhood Guide

Hua Mak and Bang Kapi, Bangkok. Rajamangala National Stadium sits on Ramkhamhaeng Road in Bang Kapi district, with no Skytrain station at the gates. Staying nearby cuts the longest leg: the Airport Rail Link's Ramkhamhaeng station and the MRT Yellow Line's Bang Kapi station, next to The Mall Bangkapi, are a short bus or taxi ride away.

Thong Lo and Ekkamai, Bangkok. For fans who want a base in the city, the Saen Saep canal boat runs from piers at Soi Thonglor and Charn Issara, at the top of Ekkamai Road, east to Mahadthai pier near the stadium. The boats stop running in the evening, so the canal works for getting there, and a taxi for getting home.

Bukit Jalil, Kuala Lumpur. TM Stadium Nasional sits in Bukit Jalil, with the Bukit Jalil LRT station on the Sri Petaling line a short walk from the gates. Staying nearby means skipping the post-show taxi queue, and the malls around the stadium keep food courts open late.

Bukit Bintang, Kuala Lumpur. For fans who want the city as well as the concert, Bukit Bintang puts Jalan Alor's hawker stalls and late-night shopping outside the door, with rail connections south to the stadium.

Kallang, Singapore. The National Stadium has its own Stadium MRT station on the Circle Line, and the Kallang waterfront gives a breezy walk before the show. Hotels in Kallang and nearby Lavender keep the trip home quick.

Senayan, Jakarta. Gelora Bung Karno sits inside Senayan, ringed by malls and served by the MRT's Istora Mandiri station. A room in Senayan or a few stops south in Blok M, with its food halls and record shops, keeps Jakarta's traffic out of the evening.

Fans can compare stays near each venue, and add flights and activities to the same booking, on Agoda.com. Travelers can enjoy Agoda's Mega Sale running from 16 November to 30 November, offering up to 60% off on hotel bookings, with a special flash sale of up to 70% on 27 November and exclusive deals on flights and activities.

SOURCE Agoda

data.title: AI is driving a flood of crypto bug reports. Now it’s helping sort them
data.description:
Crypto bug bounty platforms have expanded their use of artificial intelligence to keep up with a growing mountain of AI-assisted security reports.

Crypto-focused HackenProof said in October that it was using AI to triage 70% of submissions fully autonomously, aiming to hit 85% by the end of 2026. It said it received an average of about 6,100 bug reports a month in the third quarter, 2.4 times the reports from December last year.

Rival Immunefi last week said submissions to its platform rose 136% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, as it introduced a tool that can flag duplicates before a researcher submits a report.

Bug bounty programs pay independent researchers to find and report potential security flaws. AI has helped researchers uncover more genuine vulnerabilities, but has also swelled the volume of invalid and duplicate submissions, making it harder for security teams to identify the threats that need urgent attention.

It’s like “bringing a sword to a gunfight,” Dmitry Tokarev, founder of crypto wallet provider Bron, told Cointelegraph, referring to security teams that haven’t already adopted AI to sift through reports.

The turning point for AI-assisted bug hunting

Several bug bounty platforms have identified February as a turning point in the surge of AI-assisted vulnerability reports, coinciding with the release of more capable AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6.

HackenProof said Claude Opus 4.6 could work through larger codebases and sustain tasks for longer. HackerOne said the arrival of more capable AI models and tools in that month saw a sudden shift from a “human-only submission environment.”

Graph showing HackenProof's volume of bug reports per month. Source: HackenProof

Some crypto developers are also experimenting with financial disincentives to curb low-quality submissions.

The team behind Firedancer, a Solana validator client developed by Jump Crypto, which also uses AI to screen reports, took an additional measure in October.

To deter spam, it began requiring researchers to burn 1 SOL for each bug report they want considered for a bounty. The token is permanently destroyed, even if the report turns out to be a duplicate.

In a November update published Tuesday, HackerOne’s vice president of operations Tony Lee said they began requiring researchers to verify their identities before submitting reports in the third quarter. It also expanded its triage team and began using AI agents to automatically close clear-cut cases, such as spam and duplicate reports.

In October, it gave customers more control over how many reports their public programs receive.

Security teams brace for more bug reports and attacks

Lee said he expects vulnerability reports to keep climbing “for the foreseeable future” after recording a 22% increase in report volume in Q3 compared to the previous quarter.

Meanwhile, insurer QBE and risk consultancy Control Risks on Wednesday forecast more disruptive cyber incidents in 2027 across the 14 markets they studied, pointing to the “industrialization of AI” as one of the factors.

Mike Blank, chief product officer at blockchain infrastructure firm R3, also said he expects the number of hacks to rise sharply in 2027, but said crypto teams should pay closer attention to how much damage a single breach can cause, rather than the number of attacks.

“The real difference will be between protocols where a stolen key can drain everything and those where it can only pause operations,” Blank said.

data.title: Commodity Corner: Oil set for first weekly gain this month; gold steadies
data.description:

Oil was on track for the first weekly gain this month as attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers in the Middle East raised concerns escalating hostilities could disrupt exports.

data.title: Venezuela signs Siemens Energy deals to fix power grid
data.description:
Venezuela signed agreements with Germany's Siemens Energy in Caracas to repair and upgrade the national electricity network and the power infrastructure that serves its oil sector, Telesur reported.

Acting President Delcy Rodriguez said sanctions had prevented the grid from obtaining Siemens parts and equipment for more than 10 years.

After ten years of recurring power cuts, the government is pursuing these agreements to bring them to an end, and officials attribute the outages to a blockade led by the United States. According to the authorities, that blockade has deprived the electrical network and the oil sector alike of replacement components, technical know-how and funding.

Rodriguez tied the accords to the Venezuela Rises Plan, a development programme unveiled one day ahead of the signing, whose goals are economic stabilisation, faster growth and resolution of the national debt. Reliable power, she argued, is the foundation for attracting new investment and bringing production back.

'Venezuela’s electrical system was unable to access parts and equipment for more than a decade. In the specific case of Siemens, we could not access because of the issue of sanctions and now we are making it possible,' Rodriguez said.

Under the agreements, in which the Ministry of People's Power for Electric Energy also participated, power plants are to run more effectively and the oil sector is to make better use of its gas while meeting environmental sustainability standards. The report says that gas currently burned off or not fully exploited might instead be channelled into electricity generation, cutting waste and relieving pressure on the national grid.

Rodriguez said the bilateral deal would accelerate repairs because the electricity ministry and state oil company PDVSA had already identified exactly which components need replacing. Siemens has operated in Venezuela for over 70 years and supports a large share of its thermoelectric capacity.

Rodriguez expressed gratitude to Christian Bruch, chief executive of Siemens Energy, and to the delegation of German companies that travelled to Caracas. She gave credit to Germany's ambassador, whose diplomatic work, started two years ago, cleared the path for shared projects once more. She further remembered that after twin earthquakes hit parts of Venezuela in June, Germany dispatched rescue teams and humanitarian aid.

No timeline for the work was announced. Rodriguez ordered technical teams from state power utility Corpoelec, PDVSA and Siemens Energy to begin operations immediately.

data.title: Tokyo's core CPI hits 2.9%, strengthening case for BOJ rate hike in December
data.description:
Tokyo's consumer prices rose at their fastest pace this year in November, strengthening the case for the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to raise interest rates next month as it works to keep inflation near its 2% target.

Core consumer price index (CPI) in the capital, which leaves out volatile fresh food, climbed 2.9% from a year earlier, the highest since July 2025, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said on Friday, with the overall CPI rising 2.8%.

Tokyo's figures act as an early signal for the national picture, so the result gave the central bank fresh evidence that prices were still climbing. The measure that strips out both fresh food and energy, which the BOJ watches closely as a guide to underlying inflation, rose 2.5%.

Higher utility bills drove much of the increase, as electricity costs rose 9.5% and city gas bills climbed almost 14%, the ministry said, as summer subsidies introduced by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government came to an end. Processed food prices also rose slightly faster.

Rice offered some relief as its price fell almost 34%, the steepest drop in records dating back to 1971, after it had been a main force behind inflation a year earlier.

The data also fitted with the BOJ's recent stance, as last month, the bank judged that underlying inflation had reached a level broadly in line with its 2% goal, and it shifted its focus from pushing prices higher to keeping them steady around that level.

Government policy has however seemed to make that judgement harder as Takaichi announced last month that utility subsidies would return for three months from December, and she wants to cut the sales tax on food from April. The government also plans to scale back gasoline subsidies.

Earlier this week, the BOJ's own gauge, which removes the effect of temporary government measures, rose to 3.5% in October, its fastest in three years. Prices that businesses charge each other for services rose by the most in 36 years.

Companies have passed on higher costs linked to the West Asia conflict far more readily than in the era of long deflation and Teikoku Databank said major food and drink makers planned to raise prices on 1,477 products this month, almost ten times the number a year earlier.

Households have seemed to be the main affected with real wages, which are pay adjusted for inflation, having risen every month this year, yet consumer spending shrank for two straight quarters to September, and the government downgraded its view of consumption this week.

Governor Kazuo Ueda had said the bank would weigh the economy, inflation and financial conditions when deciding when to move. He is due to give a speech on Monday, and the BOJ announces its next rate decision on December 18.

data.title: Brent trades near month's high as Mideast conflict threatens supply
data.description:
Key points:
  • Attack on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery halts some operations
  • OPEC+ likely to roll over oil output targets for Q1
  • Russian oil refinery in Krasnodar region on fire after drone attack

By Florence Tan

Brent crude futures hovered near this month's high on Friday as ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure heightened concerns over oil exports from the conflict-hit region.

Brent crude futures fell 38 cents, or 0.39%, to $96.19 a barrel by 0140 GMT, after gaining nearly $2 on Thursday to settle at their highest since November 6.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were at $85.41 a barrel, up $1.73, or 2.07%, from their close on Wednesday. There was no settlement for WTI on Thursday due to the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We think Brent can still push above USD100/bbl without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply," ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said in a note.

Both benchmarks are headed for their first weekly gain in four weeks. Prices slipped in previous weeks on relief that US President Donald Trump did not step up military action on Iran after the US midterm elections.

However, Iran has continued to attack ships transiting the Hormuz strait, disrupting oil exports, while Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis have targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and ports.

Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck the facility on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said in a statement.

The strike was the Houthis' latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

Given the disruption from the Iran war, OPEC+ is likely to maintain its oil output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027 at a meeting on Sunday, two people with knowledge of the talks said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October with the latest incident causing a fire at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region. These attacks have hit Russia's refining output and fuel exports, tightening global diesel supplies.

Fires also hit Thailand's Bangchak refinery and Venezuela's Amuay refinery on Thursday.

Separately, an incident at the Bacalhau oilfield offshore Brazil has halted production for an estimated five to eight weeks, both the operator, Equinor , and its partner, Galp , said on Wednesday.

data.title: Philippines' trade deficit widens to a record $6.9 billion in October
data.description:
The Philippines posted its widest trade deficit on record in October, government data showed on Friday, with both exports and imports growing at the highest rate in more than five years.

  • Exports (PHEXP=ECI) rose 41.8% and imports (PHIMP=ECI) grew 50.4% on an annual basis, the Philippine Statistics Authority said, the most since April 2021

  • The value of the exports reached $10.57 billion and imports hit $17.52 billion, both the highest since record began in 1991, with the trade deficit widening to an all-time high of $6.95 billion (PHTBAL=ECI)

  • The United States was the Philippines’ biggest export market in October, taking $2.76 billion, or 26.1% of total shipments, while China remained its largest source of imports at $5.19 billion, or 29.6% of the total

  • For the first 10 months of 2026, the value of exports rose 20.1% to a record $84.71 billion, while imports increased 23.9% to a record $139.09 billion

data.title: China's industrial firms post faster profit growth as recovery remains uneven
data.description:
Profit growth at China's industrial firms accelerated in October, supported by improving conditions in parts of the manufacturing sector, although broader economic momentum remained subdued.

With domestic demand yet to gain meaningful traction and continuing to weigh on corporate earnings, many firms have increasingly relied on overseas markets for growth, leaving them vulnerable to trade tensions and geopolitical risks.

Profits at industrial firms rose 20.1% from a year earlier last month, versus a 14.4% gain in September, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday. Profits were up 16% in the first 10 months, accelerating from a 15.5% increase in the January-September period,

Industrial earnings continued to show a sharp split, with profits in computer, telecommunications and other electronic equipment manufacturing doubling in the first 10 months, while furniture manufacturing posted a decline of 52.4%.

The uneven performance comes as Beijing has introduced a series of policy measures in recent months aimed at supporting economic activity, including steps to lower borrowing costs, increase liquidity in the financial system and channel financing to sectors such as technology, manufacturing and infrastructure.

Still, analysts say the impact of the policy support has been mixed, with weak household demand and lingering strains in the property sector continuing to drag on the broader recovery.

The outlook for exports, a key source of support for manufacturers this year, has meanwhile become less certain. Concerns over potential tariff increases and other trade restrictions, particularly in the United States and the European Union, have raised questions about the sustainability of export-driven growth and the earnings prospects of firms dependent on overseas demand.

Industrial profit figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($3 million) from main operations.

($1 = 6.6722 Chinese yuan)
